articles.title: Passwords, done properly (in 6 minutes)
articles.summary: Everyone tells you to use strong passwords. Almost no one tells you how — actually.
articles.body:
Here is the entire lesson:

1. Stop memorising passwords. Use a password manager. Free options that we actually trust: Bitwarden, Proton Pass, Apple Passwords (iOS 17+).

2. One password to rule them all — your master password. Make it a passphrase of 4-6 random words. Example: 'copper-hazelnut-echo-lantern'. Length beats complexity. Never reuse this password anywhere else.

3. Turn on 2-Factor Authentication (2FA) on: Google, Apple, Microsoft, Instagram, your bank, your school. Prefer authenticator apps (Aegis on Android, Raivo/2FAS on iOS) over SMS. SMS 2FA is better than nothing but SIM-swap attacks exist.

4. Passkeys > passwords. Most big sites now support 'passkeys' (also called Passwordless / WebAuthn). Turn them on where offered. They cannot be phished.

5. Check haveibeenpwned.com — enter your email. It will tell you every breach your email is in. Change those passwords first.

6. Never reuse passwords. Your manager makes this easy.

articles.title: Spot phishing in under 10 seconds
articles.summary: The 5-check rule that catches 95% of phishing attempts.
articles.body:
Phishers rely on urgency + fear. Every phishing message has some subset of these tells:

(1) Urgency: 'Your account will be closed in 24 hours.' Real institutions rarely give you 24 hours for anything.

(2) Unusual sender: hover over the sender (or long-press on mobile). 'security@paypa1.com' vs paypal.com — the number 1 vs the letter l.

(3) Weird link previews: hover over links before clicking. If it says 'go to your bank' but shows 'bit.ly/xyz9', don't click.

(4) Attachment you didn't expect: PDFs, ZIPs, .exe — never open uninvited.

(5) They ask for a password or a code: no legitimate institution will ever ask you to send them a password, verification code, or one-time PIN via email/text.

Golden rule: if in doubt, don't click. Open a new browser tab and go to the site directly.

articles.title: Your data footprint (and how to shrink it)
articles.summary: You leak more data than you realise. Here's what leaks — and how to plug it.
articles.body:
The main leaks:

(1) Every app you install. Go to Settings → Privacy → Apps → Location/Camera/Microphone and revoke anything you don't remember using.

(2) Google + Apple accounts. Go to myaccount.google.com → Data & Privacy → 'Delete a Google service' or 'auto-delete activity' every 3 months.

(3) Third-party trackers. Install a good browser: Brave, Firefox Focus (mobile), or DuckDuckGo. Or in Safari: Settings → Safari → Privacy & Security → 'Prevent Cross-Site Tracking' ON.

(4) DNS-level ad blocking. Use NextDNS or AdGuard DNS — blocks ads + trackers at the DNS level (before they even reach your browser).

(5) Old accounts. Use justdelete.me to find delete links for services you no longer use.

articles.title: Do you need antivirus? Honest answer.
articles.summary: The 2026 truth about antivirus software — what to install, and what NOT to install.
articles.body:
The short answer:

- Windows 10/11: The built-in Microsoft Defender is genuinely good. You do NOT need paid McAfee or Norton.

- macOS: Built-in protections are strong. Optional: Malwarebytes (free) for occasional deep scans.

- Linux: Antivirus is largely unnecessary — but keep the system updated.

- Android: Google Play Protect is decent. Only install apps from Play Store or F-Droid.

- iPhone: You literally cannot install antivirus on iOS — Apple's sandbox model doesn't allow it. Don't waste money on 'iOS antivirus' apps.

What actually protects you:
1. Keep OS + apps updated (weekly).
2. Use a password manager + 2FA.
3. Don't click sketchy links.
4. Back up important files (3-2-1 rule: 3 copies, 2 media, 1 offsite).

Skip paid antivirus. Spend that money on a Bitwarden family plan instead ($40/yr for 6 people).

articles.title: Public Wi-Fi safety in 4 rules
articles.summary: The airport-cafe-hotel Wi-Fi survival kit.
articles.body:
Rule 1: If the site has HTTPS (padlock in the URL bar), you're mostly safe. Modern browsers block most public Wi-Fi snooping automatically.

Rule 2: Never install a 'certificate' a public Wi-Fi asks you to install. That's how attackers see your traffic.

Rule 3: Use a VPN for sensitive things — banking, work email, anything involving passwords. Trustworthy free VPNs: Proton VPN (free tier), Mozilla VPN (paid). Avoid random 'free VPN' apps — they often sell your data.

Rule 4: Turn OFF file-sharing / AirDrop 'Everyone' when on public networks. AirDrop → Contacts Only. Windows → 'Public network' when you connect.

Bonus: On iOS/Android, use 'Private DNS' (Settings → Network → Private DNS → dns.nextdns.io) — encrypts your DNS queries even on hostile networks.

articles.title: Social media without losing your mind
articles.summary: 6 setting changes on Instagram/TikTok/X that measurably lower anxiety.
articles.body:
Every study on teen social media anxiety points at the same handful of features. Turn these off:

(1) Read receipts (Instagram Direct, WhatsApp): Settings → Privacy → Read receipts OFF. Removes the 'why haven't they replied' spiral.

(2) Like counts: Instagram → Settings → 'Hide like and view counts' → 'Hide from posts of others'. Big impact on peer-comparison stress.

(3) Reels-first feed: Instagram → Settings → Preferences → make 'Followed' your home tab.

(4) TikTok time limit: Profile → menu → Screen Time → set daily limit (60 min).

(5) Story views: Turn off active status. IG → Settings → 'Show activity status' OFF.

(6) Notifications: Kill 'someone liked' pushes. Keep only DMs. iOS → Settings → Focus → allow specific apps only.

One meta-rule: unfollow anyone whose posts leave you feeling worse. Not muted — actually unfollowed. Life is short.

articles.title: Spotting misinformation in 60 seconds
articles.summary: A repeatable 4-step check before you share anything.
articles.body:
Before sharing any 'shocking' post, run these:

Step 1 — SIFT: Stop. Investigate the source. Find better coverage. Trace claims.

Step 2 — Reverse image search: Save the image, drop into Google Images / TinEye / Yandex. If a viral 'protest photo from Tehran 2026' is actually a 2019 photo from Beirut, you'll find out in 15 seconds.

Step 3 — Check the outlet: Type the site name into Wikipedia. If it says 'known for spreading disinformation', don't share.

Step 4 — Look for corroboration: Is the same claim in Reuters, AP, BBC, AFP? If only one obscure site has it, treat as unverified.

Rule of thumb: if a post makes you angry, wait 24 hours before sharing. Anger is the emotion misinformation targets.

articles.title: How to use ChatGPT/Gemini without becoming worse
articles.summary: The 3-rule framework for using AI that makes you smarter, not lazier.
articles.body:
Rule 1 — First draft, not last draft. Use AI to break blank-page paralysis. Then rewrite. Never submit the AI's exact words as your own.

Rule 2 — Verify everything factual. LLMs hallucinate. Cross-check every date, name, statistic, citation against a real source. Ask the AI 'what sources do you draw this from?' — then check them.

Rule 3 — Prompt like a teacher, not a customer.

Bad: 'Write me an essay on WW2.'
Good: 'Explain WW2 causes to me in 3 stages. After each stage, ask me a comprehension question. Correct me if I get it wrong.'

The second prompt makes you actually learn.

What AI is excellent at: rephrasing, summarising, brainstorming, translating, explaining concepts multiple ways.

What AI is bad at: recent events (post-training cutoff), math involving many steps, specific citations, anything requiring judgment.

articles.title: The AI ethics you actually need to know
articles.summary: 6 things every teenager using AI should know — clearly stated.
articles.body:
1) AI reflects its training data. If it's biased, that's a mirror.

2) 'Fair use' is not the same as 'permission'. Just because you can generate an image in the style of a living artist doesn't mean you should.

3) Deepfakes are illegal in most countries. Creating a fake image/video of a real person can carry criminal charges (esp. minors) in the US, UK, EU, India, Australia.

4) Your prompts are training data. Assume any private info you share with an AI could end up training its next version — unless you're on an enterprise plan.

5) Copyright of AI outputs is unsettled. In the US, purely AI outputs are NOT copyrightable. Human editing usually is.

6) Your school probably has an AI policy. Read it. Cheating via AI is still cheating — and the detectors have caught up.

articles.title: The 6 scams targeting students right now
articles.summary: The 2026 scam playbook — see them coming.
articles.body:
(1) 'You got a scholarship!' — random 'you won' emails asking for personal data or an 'application fee'. Real scholarships never ask for fees.

(2) Fake internship pages — LinkedIn 'DM me for a paid remote internship' from a stranger. Real internships come through company career pages.

(3) 'Your family member is in trouble' — voice-cloning scams. Set a family safe-word. If someone calls sounding like your mom asking for money, ask 'What's the safe word?'

(4) Crypto rug pulls in DMs — 'insider tip'. Always a scam.

(5) 'Amazon delivery' phishing SMS — link to fake pay-a-small-fee page. Amazon never asks for fees.

(6) OnlyFans / cam extortion — screenshots + threats to send to your family. Never send explicit images to anyone online. If it happens: don't pay, block, and report to takeitdown.ncmec.org (works for minors).

articles.title: Civic tech: how tech is changing government
articles.summary: Why civic tech is one of the fastest-growing career tracks.
articles.body:
Civic tech = building better software for governments + citizens.

Examples right now:
- Code for America: reduced California food-stamp application from 45 mins to 8 mins.
- Aadhaar (India): digital identity for 1.3 billion people.

articles.title: Cyberbullying: what actually works
articles.summary: A practical playbook if you're being harassed online.
articles.body:
Step 1: Screenshot everything. Timestamps + usernames. This is evidence.

Step 2: Do NOT engage. Every reply feeds the pattern.

Step 3: Block + Report. On IG/Snap/TikTok/X, use both the Block AND Report options. Reports get reviewed; blocks stop contact.

Step 4: Restrict, don't block, if you don't want them to know. 'Restrict' on Instagram makes their comments invisible to everyone but them.

Step 5: Tell one adult you trust. Not the whole world — one person. School counsellor, parent, older sibling.

Step 6: In serious cases (threats, sextortion, doxxing) go to the police. Every country has a cyber cell. India: cybercrime.gov.in. US: ic3.gov. UK: report.ceop.police.uk.

Survivor rule: what happens online is real, and it is not your fault.

articles.title: Backing up your life in 30 minutes
articles.summary: 3-2-1 backup rule for anything you'd cry over losing.
articles.body:
3-2-1 rule:
3 copies of any important file
2 different types of media (cloud + local drive)
1 offsite copy

Minimum setup for a student:
1. Google Drive / iCloud (cloud copy) — turn on Backup for photos, docs, contacts.
2. External SSD (once a month) — SanDisk 500GB is ~₹4,500. Plug in, drag Documents/Photos onto it.
3. Optional: A second cloud (Proton Drive, Sync.com) for the truly important stuff.

Do it TODAY:
- iOS: Settings → your name → iCloud → make sure iCloud Backup is ON.
- Android: Settings → System → Backup → make sure it's ON.
- Windows: File Explorer → OneDrive → sync Documents + Desktop.
- Mac: System Settings → General → Time Machine → set up an external drive.

articles.title: UPI/Venmo safety: the small habits that save you
articles.summary: How to not get scammed on payment apps.
articles.body:
Universal rules for UPI, Venmo, Cash App, PayPal, etc.:

(1) Never share your PIN or OTP. Not with 'bank customer support', not with anyone. Ever.

(2) 'Collect' vs 'Pay' — In UPI: legitimate transactions where you PAY require your PIN. If someone sends you money, they don't need your PIN. If a 'buyer' asks you to enter your PIN to 'receive' money — it's a scam.

(3) Screenshots aren't proof of payment. Always check your app's transaction history yourself.

(4) Turn ON transaction limits — UPI apps let you set daily caps. Set a low one.

(5) Use a virtual card / secondary bank account for online shopping. Keep primary savings separate.

(6) If you get scammed: report within 24 hours to your bank. In India, dial 1930 (National Cyber Crime Helpline). The faster you report, the higher chance of freezing the destination account.

links.label: India: Dial 1930 or report on cybercrime.gov.in

articles.title: Search like a researcher, not a scroller
articles.summary: Google operators that turn 4-hour research into 20 minutes.
articles.body:
The high-value operators:

- "quotes" — exact phrase. "climate finance jobs Berlin" not climate finance jobs Berlin.
- site: — restrict to a domain. site:arxiv.org quantum computing 2026.
- filetype: — filetype:pdf 'annual report'.
- - (minus) — exclude words. tesla -stock -elon.
- intitle: / inurl: — targets title or URL.
- Date filter — Tools → Any time → 'Past year'. Critical for recent events.

Beyond Google:
- Semantic Scholar — research papers with better ranking than Google Scholar.
- Perplexity.ai — AI-powered search with citations.
- Consensus.app — asks scientific questions across peer-reviewed studies.
- Wayback Machine (archive.org/web) — see any webpage as it was in the past.

articles.title: Copyright, remix, and what teens can actually use
articles.summary: A cheat sheet for legally using music/images/code in your projects.
articles.body:
Music for videos: YouTube Audio Library (free), Epidemic Sound (paid), Uppbeat, Pixabay Music.

Images: Unsplash, Pexels, Wikimedia Commons. Attribution requirements vary — always check the license.

Icons: Ionicons, Lucide, Phosphor (all free even commercially).

Fonts: Google Fonts, Fontshare. Never rip fonts.

Code: On GitHub, always read the license (MIT / Apache / GPL / Creative Commons). Copy-pasting from Stack Overflow — those answers are CC BY-SA by default → you must credit the author.

General: 'Fair use' / 'fair dealing' is a defense, not a right. Being non-commercial doesn't automatically make you safe.

If in doubt: (1) ask, (2) attribute, (3) create your own.

articles.title: Digital wellbeing: the settings that actually help
articles.summary: The five phone changes that give you an hour back a day.
articles.body:
1) Home screen — remove Instagram/TikTok/YouTube icons. Move them to page 3+. Every extra swipe is thinking time.

2) Greyscale mode — makes the phone visually boring. iOS: Settings → Accessibility → Display & Text Size → Color Filters → Grayscale. Try for a week.

3) One-Tap App Timers — iOS Screen Time / Android Digital Wellbeing. Set Instagram to 30 mins. When it hits, the app locks.

4) Focus modes — iOS Focus / Android Focus. 'Study mode' hides messages + apps you don't need.

5) Charge outside your bedroom. This is the single biggest sleep upgrade you can do. Buy a ₹500 alarm clock.

Bonus: uninstall for 24 hours. Not disable — uninstall. Notice how much your thumb tries to open it. That's the addiction pattern.

articles.title: Crypto: what teens should know (mostly: don't)
articles.summary: Honest teen-level explainer.
articles.body:
The honest version:

1) Most crypto marketing you see is designed to make someone else money at your expense.

2) 'Not your keys, not your coins.' If you use Binance/Coinbase and your account gets frozen, your money is stuck.

3) Rug pulls: >90% of new tokens launched in 2024 lost 90%+ of value within 30 days.

4) DMs about crypto = scam. Every single one.

5) If you still want to learn: put a tiny amount (₹500) into Bitcoin or Ethereum via a legitimate exchange. Sit with it for 6 months. Watch what it does emotionally. Then decide.

6) Underlying tech (blockchain, distributed systems, zero-knowledge proofs) is a legitimate CS career. That's separate from speculating on tokens.

Age-gate: In India + most countries, you legally need to be 18+ to trade crypto anyway.

articles.title: Writing online without regretting it later
articles.summary: The one rule: assume your future employer / partner / kids will read this.
articles.body:
College admissions officers, recruiters, journalists, and future partners will Google you. Assume they will find:

1) Your Instagram (public? make it private).
2) Your Twitter/X.
3) Comments on YouTube, Reddit, Discord — anything under a username you also use elsewhere.
4) Old blog posts + forum posts.

Practical rules:
- One 'public' handle used everywhere for professional stuff. LinkedIn, GitHub, portfolio.
- One 'private' handle for close-friend content. Different email, different username.
- Never post while angry, drunk, or in a fight.
- If you must vent: private group chat. Not public feed.

One trick: type your name into Google in an incognito window. That's roughly what an admissions officer sees.

articles.title: Recovering a hacked account: step by step
articles.summary: If your Instagram / Google / bank got hacked — what to do in the first 60 minutes.
articles.body:
General order:

1) Change your PRIMARY EMAIL password FIRST. If the attacker controls your email, they control every account you own.

2) Log out of all sessions everywhere (most sites have a 'sign out of all devices' button in security settings).

3) Enable 2FA if you hadn't.

4) Contact the platform's account recovery:
 - Google: g.co/recover
 - Instagram: instagram.com/hacked
 - Facebook: fb.com/hacked
 - Apple: iforgot.apple.com
 - X: help.twitter.com/en/forms/account-access/regain-access

5) Warn friends. Attackers often DM your contacts asking for money.

6) Check email forwarding rules — attackers often set a rule that forwards every email to their address.

7) Check connected apps + revoke everything you don't recognise.

8) File a report with your local cyber-crime portal if financial loss.

articles.title: Learn to code: the actually-free path
articles.summary: A 6-month self-teach path — no bootcamp fees required.
articles.body:
Month 1: CS50 (Harvard, free on edX) — you'll learn C, Python, and how a computer actually works.

Month 2: freeCodeCamp — 'Responsive Web Design' + 'JavaScript Algorithms' certifications. Free.

Month 3: Build 3 tiny projects — a to-do list, a weather app, a portfolio site. Push them to GitHub.

Month 4: Learn one back-end. FastAPI or Express.js. Build one full-stack app.

Month 5: Learn Git properly (learngitbranching.js.org — free interactive tutorial). Learn how to read documentation.

Month 6: Contribute to one open-source project on GitHub — a typo fix in README counts. This is what recruiters check.

Total cost: 0. Total value: entry-level dev jobs pay ₹8-30L/yr in India, $70-120K/yr in the US.

articles.title: Levelling up English (for non-native students)
articles.summary: TOEFL/IELTS aside — how to actually get good.
articles.body:
1) Read one long-form article per day. Recommended: Aeon, The Atlantic, Longreads, The Guardian long-reads.

2) Speak 15 minutes per day out loud. Even to yourself. Even about the weather. Fluency is a physical habit.

3) Watch shows WITH English subtitles — not your native language. The Crown, Better Call Saul, Chef's Table. Vocabulary explodes.

4) Keep a 'phrase notebook'. When you meet a phrase you didn't know, write it + one example. Review weekly.

5) Anki (spaced repetition) — flashcards for vocabulary you actually meet, not word lists.

For TOEFL/IELTS specifically:
- One month before: take a diagnostic. Buy Cambridge IELTS 18 or ETS Official Guide.
- Two weeks before: daily 2-hour practice.
- One week before: 3 full practice tests under timed conditions.
- Two days before: sleep, don't cram.

Free practice: British Council IELTS practice, Duolingo English Test (yes, some universities accept it now).

articles.title: Your first CV: what admissions actually reads
articles.summary: The CV/résumé pattern that admissions committees find easy to read.
articles.body:
Structure (top → bottom):
1) Header: Name, contact (email, one phone, city, LinkedIn if you have one).
2) Personal Statement (2 lines): 'High-school student in Bangalore. Interested in the intersection of climate + AI.'
3) Education: current school, board, exam scores (if impressive).
4) Awards & Recognitions: newest first.
5) Projects: 2-4 short bullets each — what, tech used, outcome (numbers if possible).
6) Experience: internships, volunteering, part-time work.
7) Skills: languages you speak, tools you use, code you know.
8) Interests (2 lines): interesting personal, not just 'reading books'.

Rules:
- One page.
- No photo (except for UK/EU some cases, India rarely).
- PDF, never Word doc, when submitting.
- File name: 'FirstName-LastName-CV.pdf'
- No 'objectives' section (dead pattern).
- No 'references available on request' (obvious, wastes space).

Copy-worthy templates: Overleaf CV templates (free), Novoresume free tier, ResumeGenius. Or Google Docs → Templates → Résumé.

articles.title: College application timeline (for internationals)
articles.summary: 12-month plan — starting the summer before your final year.
articles.body:
12 months out: Take diagnostic SAT/ACT + English test. Shortlist 30 universities.

11 months: Start narrowing based on cost + fit. Reach out to alumni on LinkedIn.

10 months: Book real tests (SAT, TOEFL/IELTS). Take once. Retake if needed.

9 months: First draft Common App essay. Start supplementary essays.

8 months: Line up 2-3 teachers for recommendation letters. Give them 6 weeks minimum.

7 months: Finalise your list — 5 reach, 5 target, 5 safety.

6 months (Nov): US Early Action deadlines. UK UCAS deadline.

5 months (Dec-Jan): Most US regular decision deadlines.

4 months (Feb): Australian, Singaporean applications rolling.

3 months (Mar-Apr): Decisions arrive. Compare offers.

2 months (May): Commit. Deposit.

1 month (Jun-Jul): Visa application. Housing. Financial paperwork.

Useful (free) tools: BigFuture (US colleges), UCAS (UK), Studyportals (any country), Common App.

articles.title: How to have the money conversation with your parents
articles.summary: Talking to family about going abroad — actual scripts.
articles.body:
The conversation goes better when you make it about a plan, not a want. Structure:

1) Start with a specific goal. 'I want to study X in Y country because of Z' — not 'I want to go abroad'.

2) Bring numbers. Total 4-year cost including living. Then subtract every scholarship / aid you could realistically apply for. Then subtract savings + potential loans. What's left is the real ask.

3) Show alternatives. 'If I get scholarship X it becomes ₹Y. If not, plan B is scholarship Z in country W which costs ₹A.'

4) Timeline. Show when decisions are made vs when payments start.

5) What you'll do. Part-time work rules in your target country. Post-study visa. Realistic salary after graduation.

6) Emotional part last, not first. Give them time to react.

If you're in India: the education loan ecosystem covers up to ₹1.5 crore for approved abroad programs (Prodigy Finance, Avanse, HDFC Credila, SBI). Compare rates.

Rule of thumb: total loan should be repayable in <5 years of your realistic starting salary.

articles.title: Building a personal website that pays off
articles.summary: The 3-hour personal site that actually helps you get interviews.
articles.body:
Why: recruiters + admissions Google you. If they find a coherent personal site, you look 10x more serious.

What to include:
1) Short bio (2 lines) — who you are, what you care about.
2) Photo (optional, but helps — professional-looking, not selfie).
3) 3-6 projects — each with a screenshot + 2-3 lines + a link.
4) One long-form piece — essay, blog post, YouTube video — something that shows how you think.
5) Contact (email, LinkedIn, GitHub).

What NOT to include:
- Age, marks below 90%, exhaustive skill lists, ('proficient in MS Word'? no), stock photos.

Build it in one of these (free):
- github.io (GitHub Pages) — best for coders
- notion.site — best for humanities/design
- carrd.co — best for single-page portfolios
- framer.com — best for designers

Domain name: buy your name (yourname.com or yourname.in) for ~₹800/year on Namecheap. Attach to any of the above.

articles.title: Cold-emailing that actually gets replies
articles.summary: How to email someone senior and get a reply — the honest formula.
articles.body:
Rules that work:

1) SHORT. 4-6 sentences max. If they scroll, you lose.

2) Specific. 'I loved your talk at TEDxDelhi on urban design' — not 'I love your work'.

3) Ask ONE thing. 15 minutes on the phone. A recommendation for one book. An intro to one person. Never 'can we chat about your career'.

4) Make it easy to say yes. Attach anything they'd need. Suggest 2 specific times.

5) Send Tuesday-Thursday morning. Never Monday, never Friday afternoon.

Template:

> Hi [Name],
> I'm a [year] student in [place] researching [thing they work on]. Your 2025 essay on [specific] shifted how I think about [X].
> I'm building [tiny thing] in that space. Could I ask you one question over 15 minutes on [specific date/time]?
> Either way — thank you for the essay.
> [Your name, one-line signature with a link to your site]

Expect 20-30% response rate. Send 20 emails to hear back from 5.

articles.title: Education loans in India — the honest guide
articles.summary: What actually happens when you apply for an abroad education loan.
articles.body:
Big picture: Indian banks + NBFCs will collectively finance up to ₹1.5-2 crore for approved abroad universities.

Main lenders:
1) Public banks — SBI, Bank of Baroda. Lowest interest (~9-10%), slowest process (2-3 months). Collateral often needed above ₹40L.
2) Private banks — HDFC Credila, ICICI. Middle interest (~10.5-11.5%). Faster (~3-4 weeks).
3) NBFCs — Avanse, Auxilo. Highest interest (~11-13%). Fastest (~1-2 weeks). No collateral often.
4) International — Prodigy Finance (US/UK/EU/Canada premier programs), MPower. USD-denominated. No Indian collateral, but only for specific universities.

What matters:
- Interest rate
- Moratorium (course + 6-12 months where you don't pay)
- Prepayment penalty (avoid loans that penalise early repayment)
- Whether interest accrues during moratorium (usually yes — factor into total cost)

Comparison sites: Vidya Lakshmi (government portal), Bank Bazaar, Paisa Bazaar.

Tax benefit: Section 80E — interest on education loan is fully deductible from taxable income (no upper limit) for up to 8 years.
